theme: The ark in Philistia; its return; Samuel judges Israel
readingInstruction: Read 1 Samuel 5:1-7:17. The ark, captured in chapter 4, now travels through Philistine cities and comes home. Then Samuel leads Israel in repentance. Notice who is in control throughout.
settingTheScene: The Philistines have captured the ark and taken it to the temple of Dagon in Ashdod. These chapters show what happens next. The ark is not a trophy. It is the throne of the LORD, and he defeats Dagon without an army. After seven months, the Philistines send it back with an offering. At Kiriath-jearim it rests for twenty years. Then Samuel calls Israel to turn from idols and leads them to a decisive victory at Mizpah.
observation: The Philistines set the ark beside Dagon, and the next morning Dagon has fallen on his face before the ark (5:1-3).
The next morning, Dagon is on the ground again, with head and hands cut off (5:4).
The LORD afflicts the people of Ashdod, Gath, and Ekron with tumors, and they say, “The hand of his is heavy against us” (5:6-12).
The Philistine priests advise sending the ark back with a guilt offering, to test whether the LORD is responsible (6:1-9).
Two cows pull the cart straight to Beth-shemesh, “lowing as they went” (6:10-12).
Some of the men of Beth-shemesh look into the ark, and God strikes them. They say, “Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God?” (6:19-20).
Samuel says, “If you are returning to the LORD with all your heart, then put away the foreign gods” (7:3).
Samuel sets up a stone and calls it Ebenezer, saying, “Till now the LORD has helped us” (7:12).
interpretation:
The story of the ark in Philistia is told with a touch of dark humor. The god Dagon bows to the ark of the LORD, falls, and breaks. The Philistines suffer plagues. And the cows, who have never pulled a cart, walk straight to Israel with their calves left behind. The point is that the LORD does not need anyone’s help. He was not defeated at Aphek. He allowed Israel to be defeated, and he is still the God above all gods. The loss of the ark was not his defeat, but his judgment.

The lesson for Israel is double. First, God cannot be used. The Philistines learn that the ark cannot be treated as a prize. The men of Beth-shemesh learn that the ark cannot be treated casually, either. God’s holiness cuts both ways. The cry of the men of Beth-shemesh, “Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God?” is the question that the whole law raises.

The turning point is chapter 7. After twenty years, the people lament after the LORD. Samuel’s answer is simple and direct: if you are returning with all your heart, put away the foreign gods. Repentance is not just sorrow. It is the removal of idols. Israel obeys, they fast and confess at Mizpah, and when the Philistines attack, the LORD thunders from heaven and routs them. The people do nothing but cry out. God fights for them.

The stone Ebenezer, “stone of help,” is a monument of memory. “Till now the LORD has helped us.” It is a statement of gratitude and also of confidence about the future. If he has helped us thus far, he will not stop. The hymn “Come, Thou Fount” echoes this verse.

Samuel judges Israel throughout his life, going on a circuit each year. This is the beginning of a leader who is not a warrior but a man of prayer.
connection: Paul says that “what agreement has the temple of God with idols?” (2 Corinthians 6:16). Jesus is greater than the ark; he is the true presence of God with us. John 1:14 says that the Word “dwelt” among us. Hebrews 12:28-29 calls God a consuming fire. 1 John 5:21 ends with, “Little children, keep yourselves from idols.”
application:
Name one “Ebenezer” in your own story, a place where you can say, “Till now the LORD has helped me.”

Ask whether there is a foreign god you need to put away: something you trust more than God.

Remember that God is not defeated when things seem to go wrong. He is working.
prayerPrompts: Put away a foreign god in your own life, by naming it before God.
Return to him with all your heart, and say what that means today.
Thank him for helping you thus far.
